serpGaps: Half of page 1 is image galleries and template libraries (dribbble, figma, mobbin, pinterest). They show what chat windows look like, not how to decide what the bot does. Our post is a decision-first method.
IBM (#3) defines the discipline and splits UI from UX, but it is a definition page written for enterprise buyers of IBM tooling; no step order, no LLM answer states, no testing method.

NN/g (#7) gives guidelines for site-specific AI chatbots (capabilities, prompt suggestions, page context). It is an unordered list for websites, not an in-product SaaS assistant method, and it does not cover US disclosure law or accessibility of streamed replies.
No ranking page asks the first question: does this product need a chatbot, or a better screen? Our Step 1 decision flow fills that gap.

Example lists (sendbird, eleken, lazarev, arounda) critique screenshots. None gives a scope artifact; we add a one-job card (trigger phrases, details to collect, answer format, success signal, fallback).
Repair is reduced to 'add a fallback'. We cite Google's reprompt guidance and set a two-failed-turn handoff rule from our own published practice.

LLM-specific design (streaming, sources, confidence cues, refusals, wrong-but-confident answers) is missing from the older pages (Intercom 2021). We cover it with Google PAIR's error framing and our AI UX patterns.

No page covers the US frame: California's bot disclosure law (§17941) and WCAG 2.2 AA for chat (4.5:1 contrast, SC 4.1.3 status messages for 'typing' and streamed text) with ADA/Section 508 as context.

Testing advice stops at 'test and iterate'. We give a transcript scorecard with written pass thresholds (task success, turns per task, handoff rate, wrong-answer catches) set by the team before sessions.
Format gap: nothing on page 1 is a checklist with a pass gate per step; ours is, and the 8 gates are the TOFU lead asset.

contentModules.title: Chatbot design: an 8-step checklist for SaaS and AI product teams
contentModules.subtitle: How to design a chatbot or AI assistant that people finish tasks with: decide if chat fits, scope its first jobs, write the happy and repair paths, show sources, design every reply state, set handoff rules, meet US accessibility and disclosure rules, and test with transcripts. Each step ends with a pass gate.
contentModules.intro: Three-question gate opener (see variety.introStyle): Saliha's first sentence carries the keyword and lists the three questions she asks before opening Figma (What job will people bring to it? What happens when it is wrong? Who takes over?), as one sentence with an inline numbered list, not a blockquote. Then the IBM-based definition of chatbot design in one sentence (first 60 words), the Pew 34% line as the reason chat is now expected, and a one-line map of the 8 steps. First UP link to the hub inside the first 300 words.

dataModules.what: Chat or screen? 4 yes/no questions → 3 outcomes: improve the screen or form; guided bot with buttons; open AI assistant with free text.

A card for one job of the hypothetical product: job name, trigger phrases from transcripts, details to collect, answer format, success signal, fallback, owner. Plus a short ranked job list (text table: job | share of transcripts | answer source | launch? yes/later).
Table: turn | happy path | repair path, 5 rows for one job, introduced by one sentence and a 'Table:' line.
One assistant reply drawn in 7 states: streaming, answer with source, low confidence, refusal, error with retry, offline, handoff, each with its next action.
Numbered handoff triggers (asked for a person, two failed turns, sensitive topic, account/payment action, negative sentiment) + what context passes to the agent.
Columns: task | pass threshold (team-set) | result | turns | handoff? | wrong answer caught? | verdict. Illustrative rows for the hypothetical product, labeled as an example; no benchmark rates.
Step | gate question | pass when… One row per step; the TOFU checklist download mirrors it.

outline.h2: Step 1: Does your product need a chatbot, or a better screen?
outline.answerHint: **A product needs a chatbot when users bring open-ended questions in their own words and the answer sits in content they cannot easily browse; when the task has fixed fields, a better screen or form beats chat.** (≤40 words)
points: First H2 is a decision, not a definition (audit 2026-10-19). The definition already sits in the intro.

Chat-or-screen decision flow (visual 1 + astext): 4 questions (Do users phrase the request many ways? Is the answer in docs, data or policy they would otherwise search? Does the task need back-and-forth to collect details? Can a person take over when it fails?) → 3 outcomes.
Support bot vs AI assistant in one sentence each, then deep link to the hub comparison (conditional internal target) instead of rebuilding the hub's 5-row table.
NN/g: one chat entry point, not an AI chat beside a separate live chat (eav[5]).

Hypothetical example introduced here and used through the post: a US payroll and scheduling SaaS for restaurant groups adding an assistant that answers 'why is my paycheck different this week?' and 'can I swap Friday's shift?'. Label it hypothetical. Paycheck questions → assistant; shift swap → a better screen with a deep link from chat.
Gate 1 line at the end: 'Pass when you can name the screen the bot replaces or the search it shortcuts.'
Bridge: 'If chat wins, the next question is which jobs it takes first.'

outline.h2: Step 2: Which jobs should the chatbot handle on day one?
outline.answerHint: **Launch the chatbot with the few jobs that make up most of your real support chats or searches, each with a known answer source, and park the rest for later.**
points: Where jobs come from: transcripts and search logs (eav[7]); the words users actually use become trigger phrases. Carry 'design chatbot' here (keywordCarrier.secondary).
Scope fact: a support widget with 20 to 30 intents is the small end of our work (eav[6]); state as our published scope, link the hub cost section later, not here.

One-job scope card (visual 2 + astext) for 'explain a paycheck difference': trigger phrases, details to collect (pay period, location), answer format (answer card with line items), success signal, fallback, owner on the payroll team.
Ranked job list as a text table with 'launch / later' decision (illustrative shares labeled as example, not data).
Starter prompts come from the top jobs: NN/g says helpful bots state capabilities and offer relevant prompt suggestions (eav[4]).
Gate 2: 'Pass when every launch job has an answer source and an owner.'
Bridge: 'With the jobs fixed, write how each conversation goes, and how it goes wrong.'

outline.h2: Step 3: How do you write the happy path and the repair paths?
outline.answerHint: **Write each job's conversation twice: the happy path in as few turns as possible, then the repair path for every turn where the bot can misunderstand, stall or lack data.**
points: Happy path: greeting that states what the bot can do, collect details with suggested replies instead of typing, answer in a card, confirm, offer the next step.
Repair path: Google's reprompt guidance (eav[8]): first reprompt short and not a word-for-word repeat; second adds options or examples; then hand off (eav[9]).
Two-lane path table (text table) for one job, 5 turns. Introduce with one sentence and a 'Table:' line.

Tone and length: short replies, one question per turn; a personality guide fixes greeting, length and tone (link the hub deliverable 'Bot personality guide' only if the link budget allows; otherwise plain mention).
Mention once that the silo's deeper conversation-writing guide is planned (no link, no promise of date). Do NOT target 'chatbot conversation design' here.
Gate 3: 'Pass when every turn has a repair line and no repair loops back to the same question twice.'
Bridge: 'Rule-based bots stop there. An LLM assistant adds a new problem: answers that sound right and are not.'

outline.h2: Step 4: How does AI chatbot design show where an answer came from?
outline.answerHint: **AI chatbot design shows the source of each answer, a plain-language confidence cue and a one-tap way to correct or reject it, so users can check the answer before they act on it.**
points: Why: LLM output differs each time and can be confidently wrong; Google PAIR's three error questions (eav[12]).
Patterns: source link or quote under the answer, 'based on your March 14 pay stub' style grounding, confidence wording, feedback buttons, edit/regenerate (eav[11]).
The post's ONE cross-hub link: our AI UX design agency team designs these review and correction patterns (eav[11]).
Streaming: generation takes 3 to 20 seconds (eav[10]); stream text and show progress rather than a spinner.
Pillar mention: /services/ai-products/ (AI product design) once, in the sentence on trust.
Gate 4: 'Pass when every AI answer that can trigger an action shows its source.'
Bridge: 'Sources cover the good answer. The next step covers every other state a reply can be in.'

outline.h2: Step 5: Which states does every chatbot reply need?
outline.answerHint: **Every chatbot reply needs a designed state for streaming, a sourced answer, low confidence, refusal, error with retry, offline and handoff, and each state ends with one clear next action.**
points: First sentence after the bold answer carries 'chatbot interaction design' (keywordCarrier.secondary).
Reply state strip (visual 3 + astext), the hypothetical paycheck answer in 7 states.
Link the hub's 'System states' deliverable via the hub include section (conditional) instead of listing the hub's 6 parts.
Refusal copy says what the bot cannot do and what to try next; error copy keeps the user's typed message.
LEAD ANGLE 1 lives at the end of this section (see leadAngle).
Gate 5: 'Pass when no state ends without a next action.'
Bridge: 'One of those states is a person.'

outline.h2: Step 6: When should the chatbot hand off to a person?
outline.answerHint: **Hand off to a person when the user asks for one, after two failed turns, and before any sensitive or irreversible action, and pass the full chat history so the user never repeats themselves.**
points: Handoff rule list as an ol (text): asked for a person; two failed turns (eav[9]); pay, legal, health or account-closure topics (Microsoft guideline, eav[17]); negative sentiment; outside hours → ticket with expected reply time.
What passes to the agent: the job, details collected, the bot's last answer and its source.
Visible handoff button from the first message, not hidden behind failure.
Do NOT reuse the handoff ladder visual or wording from /blog/user-onboarding-automation/ (other silo).
Gate 6: 'Pass when a tester can reach a person in two taps from any state.'
Bridge: 'Handoff protects users who are stuck. The next step protects users who cannot see the screen and users who need to know it is a bot.'

outline.h2: Step 7: How do you make chatbot design accessible and lawful in the US?
outline.answerHint: **Make chatbot design accessible by meeting WCAG 2.2 AA (4.5:1 text contrast, keyboard use and screen reader announcements for new messages), and lawful by stating clearly that users are talking to a bot.**
points: Contrast 4.5:1 / 3:1 (eav[14]); our chat windows target at least 4.5:1 for message text (hub FAQ).

SC 4.1.3 Status Messages (eav[15]): announce 'typing', streamed answers and errors through a live region without moving focus; avoid announcing every streamed token (announce when the answer completes). Keyboard: focus stays in the input after send.

faqs.q: What are the four types of chatbots?
faqs.a: Teams usually group chatbots by how they understand input: menu or button bots, rule-based keyword bots, intent-based bots trained on example phrases, and generative AI assistants built on a large language model. Many products mix two, such as buttons for known jobs and free text for the rest.

faqs.q: What is the difference between chatbot UI and UX design?
faqs.a: UX design decides what the bot says, which actions it offers and when a person takes over; UI design decides how that dialogue looks: layout, buttons, input and window size (IBM's split). Our hub page covers the interface side as chatbot interface design.

faqs.q: What are the core chatbot design principles?
faqs.a: Chatbot design principles in one line each: say what the bot can do, keep replies short, offer suggested replies, show sources for AI answers, repair before you repeat, hand off after two failed turns, and announce new messages to screen readers.

faqs.q: How long does chatbot design take?
faqs.a: With our team, 3 to 8 weeks: transcript review, flow design, interface design and conversation testing. A narrow FAQ bot sits at the short end; an assistant across web and mobile with file uploads sits at the long end.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to design a chatbot?
faqs.a: Our published range is $15,000 to $60,000, depending on the number of intents, channels and languages; link the hub cost section and do not add any other price.

faqs.q: Can I design a chatbot without a designer?
faqs.a: Yes, for a narrow FAQ bot in a builder tool, if you follow the 8 gates. The usual gaps are repair paths, AI answer states, handoff and screen reader support, which is where a designer saves rework.
